messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Keller, a 50-year-old married psychologist, came to treatment after months of telling himself that he should be able to handle this on his own. He had spent years sitting across from other people’s pain in his office, listening carefully, finding language for what overwhelmed them. What unsettled him now was that when he turned toward his own experience, language seemed to disappear. He could describe schedules, symptoms, and practical disruptions, but the central event stopped him. He would begin to approach it internally and then feel himself pull away before the memory became complete, as if some mental door slammed shut just before he could see the whole thing. What remained was often not a picture at all but a surge of feeling that arrived in his body with full force—terror, humiliation, a sickening sense of being overrun—without any clear image to anchor it.

The assault had happened after an evening in which alcohol was present, and the smell of it had fixed itself in his mind in a way he never expected. He could not narrate the event in a smooth sequence, even in the privacy of his own thoughts. What he could convey was the intimate immediacy of certain fragments: the odor of alcohol on another person’s breath and skin, the engulfing certainty that his own personhood had disappeared, the experience of being handled as though he were not a man with a mind and will but a thing to be used. In the aftermath, sirens became charged as well. If an ambulance passed while he was walking downtown or if a police car cut through traffic outside his office with its siren on, he felt a sharp internal jolt before he knew what had happened. The sound seemed to rip open the same state of alarm, and for several moments he was no longer simply hearing a siren on a city street; he was seized by the emotional intensity of the assault, even when no visual memory came with it.

In the weeks that followed, Martin noticed changes that he found difficult to admit, especially to himself. He had long thought of himself as thoughtful, articulate, and emotionally available in his work and in his marriage. Now he often felt dead inside. His wife would ask a simple question about his day and get back a flat, abbreviated answer. Sitting with patients, he could still perform the outward tasks of therapy, but there were sessions in which he felt detached from both them and himself, as though he were moving through practiced motions with the vital part missing. In private moments he had come to believe that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. It was not only that he felt shaken; it was that the capacities he most valued—putting experience into words, staying present with emotion, inhabiting his role with steadiness—now seemed inaccessible when they mattered most.

His daily environment repeatedly exposed him to reminders he could not reliably control. As a psychologist, he worked in a professional office building near a busy street, and sirens were common enough that he began bracing whenever traffic noise shifted. He found himself becoming wary in subtler ways too, orienting to discomfort before he even understood it. If he noticed the faint smell of alcohol in a hallway after another tenant’s lunch, or on a patient who mentioned having had a drink the night before, his body tightened and his attention narrowed. He did not always identify the source in the moment; sometimes it began simply as a feeling of being uncomfortable, an internal wrongness that made him want to leave the room, shorten the session, open a window, or move farther away. Over time these moments accumulated. He adjusted his schedule where he could, avoided professional gatherings where drinks would be served, and became more rigid about his physical surroundings at work. Those changes were visible enough that colleagues noticed he was turning down invitations and keeping more to himself.

At home, the consequences were harder for him to hide. His wife experienced him as present in body but absent in spirit, and Martin knew she was right. What frightened him most was not only the return of these states when something set him off, but the conviction that the assault had altered him at a basic level. He was certain, in his darkest moments, that he had been reduced to an object during the rape and had never fully become a person again afterward. Seeking help required tolerating the very thing he had been unable to do alone: approaching an experience he could not fully recall and could barely name. He came in because the numbness was spreading through too much of his life, because the sound of sirens outside his office could still undo him in an instant, and because he wanted, more than anything, to find some way to feel like a person again without being overwhelmed by what happened.
